title: Sweet Fibre: Impact of sugar replacement on blood glucose and the gut microbiome
official: Impact of replacement of sugar with fermentable fibre on glycaemia and gut microbiome function and composition
summary:
Background and study aims
Many people consume more sugar than recommended, which can contribute to health problems such as obesity, tooth decay and type 2 diabetes. One way to reduce sugar intake is to replace some sugar in foods with dietary fibre. Dietary fibre is found naturally in foods such as fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and legumes. Fibre cannot be fully digested by the body. Instead, it reaches the large intestine, where it is broken down by gut bacteria. This process produces substances that may have beneficial effects on gut health and metabolism.

Researchers have developed a new fibre-rich sugar alternative made from plant materials that would otherwise be considered agricultural waste products. Before this ingredient can be used more widely, it is important to understand how it affects blood sugar levels and the gut microbiome in humans. This study will investigate whether replacing some sugar in chocolate with this novel fibre-rich ingredient influences blood glucose levels, gut bacteria and the substances they produce. 

The aim of this study is to investigate how replacing sugar with a novel fibre-rich sugar alternative affects blood glucose levels, the composition of the gut microbiome and the activity of gut bacteria in healthy adults.

Who can participate?
Healthy non-smoking adults aged 18 to 65 years living in the United Kingdom.

What does the study involve?
Participants will take part in two separate 7-day study periods. During one study period, they will eat chocolate containing a novel fibre-rich sugar alternative. During the other study period, they will eat a similar chocolate containing standard sugar. The order of the two study periods will be decided at random. The study periods will be separated by a break of at least 14 days for men and up to 28 days for women.

Throughout each study period, participants will record what they eat and drink, their bowel habits and any digestive symptoms they experience. They will also provide stool and urine samples for laboratory analysis. At the end of each study period, participants will attend a study visit where blood and breath samples will be collected before and after eating a study chocolate product. Researchers will use these samples to measure blood glucose responses and assess changes in gut bacteria and the substances they produce.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive a direct health benefit from taking part. However, the results could help researchers develop healthier food products with lower sugar levels and higher fibre content. Some participants may experience temporary digestive symptoms, such as changes in bowel habits or mild gastrointestinal discomfort, when consuming additional dietary fibre. Blood sampling may also cause temporary discomfort, bruising or mild pain at the collection site.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being conducted by the University of Glasgow in Scotland, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
Participant recruitment began in April 2026 and is expected to continue until December 2026. The study is expected to finish in March 2027.

Who is funding the study?
Innovate UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prof Douglas Morrison, University of Glasgow,  douglas.morrison@glasgow.ac.uk.

interventions.name:
Participants: Healthy adults

Sex ratio: 1:1 M/F

Interventions:
Control: Chocolate containing 40% cane sugar
Intervention: Chocolate containing 20% beet sugar and 20% "sweet fibre"

Sweet fibre is a combination of Xylo-oligosaccharides, Cellobiose and Cellulose products

Dose: 2 x chocolate bars co

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Self-reported healthy adults (aged 18+)
2. Non-smokers
Exclusion criteria:
1. Individuals with any allergies or conditions affecting bowel health e.g. inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis), irritable bowel syndrome, coeliac disease or diverticular disease
2. Individuals who are pregnant or are trying to get pregnant
3. Individuals who have taken antibiotics in the past 3 months
4. Individuals who are taking medication that may modify gastrointestinal function e.g. prokinetic agents (e.g. metoclopramide), anti-emetics, Proton pump inhibitors, constipation treatments (e.g. lactulose, polyethylene glycol)
